title: New Best Friend
full_review:
New Best Friend" (TriStar) may have clinched the race for worst picture of 2002, reaching theaters nearly three years after filming wrapped.

Predictable when it isn't muddled, the film is an embarrassment to all associated with it. The dreadful drama is set on a Southern college campus where the local sheriff, Artie Bonner (Taye Diggs) investigates whether a shy, bookish student, Alicia (Mia Kirshner), lying near death in the hospital, accidentally overdosed on pure cocaine or was the victim of attempted murder.

Not one true note is rung in this awful mess of a movie. Initially plain and ridiculously frumpy, Alicia is immediately transformed into a gorgeous, kittenish co-ed by her newfound "friends." These friends are the popular girls on campus: poor-little-rich-girl Hadley (Meredith Monroe), bulimic Julianne (Rachel True) and sex-obsessed Sydney (Dominique Swain). Alicia and Hadley are paired to work together on a class sociology project, which is the impetus for their friendship and the reason Alicia is brought into the fold.

The pseudo-thriller has Diggs, outfitted in an array of colorful short-sleeved shirts, poking around campus in what must be one of the most ineffectual investigations in movie history. Sheriff Artie walks into Alicia's room and basically pilfers evidence hoping to catch a break. Maybe his stupid behavior is supposed to be excused because, as explained the Sheriff's voice-over narration at the opening of the film, nothing ever happens in the sleepy Carolina town. So how is he supposed to know how to act in a criminal investigation? Poor Diggs, he walks around looking as lost as the script is.

Several unintentional laughs may be the only thing that keeps the audience interested or awake. "New Best Friend" is so awful that watching the film begins to feel like a surreal experience. Could I really be watching such a terrible film? Or am I trapped in some masochistic nightmare? The amateurish narrative plods along interminably. The caricatured characters spout nonsensical dialogue. And the whole movie is layered with gratuitous sex scenes including one involving two women filmed with out of focus, psychedelic camera angles. And director Zoe Clarke-Williams uses every silly camera trick -- slow motion viewing as Alicia's crush Trevor (Scott Bairstow) walks by -- in an attempt to distract viewers from the dim-witted script.

Finally, the clueless Sheriff pieces it all together, in an ending unworthy of even a "Scooby-Do" episode, and solves the mystery. Moviegoers, you have been well warned!

Due to several gratuitous sexual situations including same-sex kissing, some nudity, sporadic drug use and intermittent rough language with brief profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
